paragraphs: New Terminology of MASLD
Steatotic Liver Disease (SLD)

Steatotic Liver Disease (SLD) is an umbrella term used to describe all individuals with excess (greater than 5% of hepatocytes) hepatic fat content in the liver detected by liver imaging or biopsy. In the past, patients with steatosis of the liver who did not drink excessively were considered to have non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). The rationale to change the terminology from NAFLD included the reliance on exclusionary diagnostic criteria and concerns regarding potential stigmatization (terms like "non-alcoholic” and “fatty”).

In 2023, a multi-society Delphi consensus statement was published defining the new nomenclature.   The pathophysiology of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) is believed to be largely driven by insulin resistance and other cardiometabolic risk factors. (Rinella et al, 2023)
SLD is an umbrella term for MASLD, ALD, and MetALD. The old terminology allowed for only two group classifications- NAFLD & ALD.
SLD is sub-classified into sub-phenotypes based on the underlying etiology and pathophysiology as follows:
Rinella ME, Lazarus JV, Ratziu V, et al. A multisociety Delphi consensus statement on new fatty liver disease nomenclature. J Hepatol. 2023;79(6):1542-1556.
SLD is sub-classified into sub-phenotypes based on the underlying etiology and pathophysiology as follows:

MASLD: Individuals with hepatic steatosis and at least 1 cardiometabolic risk factor who consume  <1.5 drinks/day (in females)/<2 drinks/day (in males). The quantity roughly translates to 20/30 g (females/males) daily or 140/210 g (females/males) weekly.

MASH is a sub-phenotype of MASLD which is associated with inflammation with or without fibrosis. MASH patients with F2-F4 fibrosis are at a significantly higher risk of liver related events and mortality compared to those with F0 or F1 and are deemed “at risk MASH”.
Clinically significant fibrosis (CSF) is a sub-phenotype of MASH with stage 2 fibrosis or higher.2

MetALD: Individuals with hepatic steatosis and at least 1 cardiometabolic risk factor who consume  2 - 3.5 drinks/day in females/2 – 4.5 drinks/day in males. The quantity roughly translates to 35/45 g (females/males) daily or 140/210 g (females/males) weekly.3

ALD: Individuals with hepatic steatosis whose liver disease is believed to be primarily due to excessive alcohol intake via consumption of  > 3.5 drinks (in females)/> 4.5 drinks (in males). The quantity roughly translates to 50/60 (f/m) daily or 140/210 (f/m) weekly.4

Drug induced Steatotic Liver Disease:  Individuals with hepatic steatosis believed to be due to the effect of a steatogenic medication such as: corticosteroids, methotrexate, amiodarone, tamoxifen, valproate, or 5-fluorouracil to name a few.5
Other causes of SLD include: Malnutrition, Celiac disease, Wilson disease.
In the United States, a “standard alcohol drink" is defined as any of the following: (by National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA)):
12 ounces of 5% ABV Beer
5 ounces of 12% ABV wine
1.5 ounces of 40% (80 proof) ABV distilled spirits (gin, run, vodka or whiskey)
ABV (alcohol by volume) refers to the strength of the alcoholic beverage
Patient self-report of alcohol intake is frequently inaccurate or underreported.
Phosphatidyl ethanol (PEth) is a serum-based biomarker test that quantifies ethanol metabolites (Vaz, et al., 2025)
Serum PeTH levels correlate with the amount of alcohol consumption over the prior 1-4 weeks.
This objective quantitative tool can be considered for use in conjunction with alcohol use screening and monitoring (Vaz, et al., 2025).
Serum PeTh level measurements may help differentiate MASLD versus MetAld, which can lead to optimized treatment plans.
Epidemiology of MASLD
Mortality Rate in MASLD
MASLD is associated with a 2-fold higher overall mortality rate compared to non-MASLD patients in the general population. (Simon, et al 2021)
Among those with MASLD, the all-cause mortality rate and liver related complications increase with  increasing severity of hepatic fibrosis rather than the steatosis grade. (Sanyal et al, 2021)
There is a marked increase in all-cause mortality for stage 3 fibrosis (Hazard Ratio (HR): 2.8 (95% CI: 1.4 – 5.4) and cirrhosis (HR: 5.6 (95% CI: 2.8 – 11.5) compared to early stage fibrosis (≤ 2)
There is also a marked increase in hepatic decompensation and associated mortality starting at stage 3 fibrosis (HR: 18.3 (95% CI: 5.4 – 62.6) and cirrhosis (HR: 52.8 (95% CI: 15.5 – 180.2)
(Sanyal et al, 2021)
Prevalence of steatotic liver disease, MASLD, MetALD and ALDin the United States based upon the NHANES 2017 to 2020 survey
MASLD severity and risk of liver disease progression

Making  an accurate distinction is important since patients with simple steatosis are at low risk for liver related events, while those with MASH and advanced fibrosis are at increased risk for liver as well as cardiovascular related morbidity and mortality.
Therefore, knowing the severity of fibrosis in MASH is essential to identify subjects in need of lifestyle or pharmaceutical interventions.
MASH progresses in severity of fibrosis, at an average of 1 stage of fibrosis every 7 years and more rapidly, at an average of 2 years, between stage 3 fibrosis to cirrhosis.
MASH patients with F2-F4 fibrosis are at a significantly higher risk of liver related events and mortality compared to those with F0 or F1 and are deemed “at risk MASH”.
Regression of fibrosis and cirrhosis by 1 stage or more from treatment has been associated with up to a 6-fold reduction in liver related events.

A 1 to 2 cm percutaneous liver biopsy can confirm the presence and severity of hepatic steatosis, liver inflammation and degree of hepatic fibrosis.  However, limitations of liver biopsy include its  potential for sampling artifact along with its invasive nature and potential for severe complications as well as associated costs. The severity of hepatic fibrosis can be quantified using a trichrome stain and graded on a scale of F0 (no fibrosis) to F4 (cirrhosis).
Prevalence of MASLD
MASLD is highly prevalent in the US and other western countries, affecting up to a third of all adults.

The pathophysiology of MASLD is believed to arise in the setting of insulin resistance associated with cardiometabolic risk factors such as obesity, diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia that results in hepatic steatosis identified on liver imaging or liver biopsy.

MASLD is underdiagnosed in the general population and in specialist care settings including cardiology, endocrine, and metabolic medicine practices due to its asymptomatic nature with frequently normal liver biochemistries. (Loomis, et. al. 2018, Lazaruss, et. al., 2025)

In MASLD, disease activity is determined by the extent of hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and hepatocyte ballooning on a liver biopsy. The majority of patients with non-cirrhotic MASLD do not have any clinical symptoms such as abdominal pain, fatigue, or pruritus.
The prevalence of MASLD is anticipated to further increase  in the US going from 86.3 (33.7%) to 122 (4.14%) million people in 2050
(Le, P et al, 2025)

In addition, the number of patients with ≥ F2 MASH is expected to increase from 6.7 to 11.7 million people which will lead to 22, 440 new cases of HCC and 6720 cases needing liver transplant per year through 2050
(Le, P et al, 2025)

Histological findings in MASLD. Patients with MASLD may have simple steatosis or steatosis with inflammation and hepatocyte ballooning termed "Steatohepatitis". The severity of hepatic fibrosis in MASLD can be determined using a Mason Trichrome stain where the blue colored fibers represent collagen tissue. The Metavir fibrosis scoring system varies from F0 (no collagen), F1 (Perisinusoidal or portal fibrosis), F2 (Sinusoidal and portal or periportal fibrosis) F3 (Septal and bridging fibrosis) and F4 (cirrhosis)
Identify High Risk Patients
In clinical practice, primary care providers should try to identify high risk patients who may have underlying MASLD/ MASH based upon their medical history, and alcohol history.
Screening for MASLD:
1. Studies of patients with MASLD in primary care settings demonstrate a lower rate of clinically significant fibrosis (≥F2)  compared to patients seen in specialty clinics.
2. Due to the documented high proportion of individuals with type 2 diabetes and obesity who have MASLD, the AASLD recommends screening for MASLD in all individuals with
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus
Obesity defined as BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2
≥ 2 Metabolic Syndrome Features
Hepatic Steatosis
Family History of Cirrhosis
Mild Alcohol Consumption
3. Similarly, all patients with suspected MASLD should be screened for occult diabetes mellitus and alcohol consumption (Rinella 2023)
A two step screening pathway offers a cost-effective strategy to
a. screen the  large at-risk population and identify those who need further screening for advanced fibrosis.
b. rule out individuals at low risk for advanced fibrosis with low cost primary testing (Fib-4 index).

c. apply secondary testing to identify individual who are still at moderate or high risk for advanced fibrosis.  The latter group should be considered for referral to Gastroenterology & Hepatology as they would benefit from further evaluation in specialty care and treatment.
Rationale for two-step screening pathway proposed by AASLD (Samala, N.)
Step 1: Calculate a Fib-4 Index
Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) Index
FIB-4 is the initial non-invasive test (NIT) to assess for advanced liver fibrosis in patients with known or suspected MASLD. It can also be used for the assessment of fibrosis.
The simple and well-validated FIB-4 formula utilizes labs frequently obtained in primary care.
The FIB-4 provides risk stratification to identify those at low, moderate, or high risk for  advanced liver fibrosis, with cut-off ranges for those between age 35-65 years, as follows:

Limitations of Fib-4
FIB-4 is not precise enough to distinguish between individual stages of hepatic fibrosis (I.e. F1, F2, F3, F4), but is useful for ruling in/out advanced fibrosis (> F3).
FIB-4 performs better in non-diabetic patients for excluding advanced fibrosis (F3/F4)  compared to diabetics.
FIB-4 risk stratification scoring ranges may need to be adjusted for those with obesity or type II diabetes  to optimize clinical capture of target population.
FIB-4 scoring is primarily intended for those aged 35-65.
Older age inflates FIB-4 score due to age being part of the equation.
If applied to a patient > 65 years of age, the lower limit of moderate risk range is adjusted up to 2.0 from 1.3.
The FIB-4 is less accurate in those below 35 years of age, so secondary assessment is recommended in those at risk or with abnormal liver chemistries in this age group.
(Rinella et al., 2023; Ito et al., 2023; Cusi, et al., 2022).

Step 2: When Fib-4 is ≥ 1.3
Clinicians should order either an Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) serum panel or Vibration Controlled Transient Elastography (VCTE) to further screen the patient and determine the next steps.
Step 2: When Fib-4 is ≥ 1.3
The Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) serum panel:

ELF is a is a blood based test, calculated using the individual components hyaluronic acid, tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1, and N-terminal procollagen III peptide. It can be done in labs with access to Siemens software. However, it underperforms in low prevalence settings and can vary with the presence of metabolic syndrome. (Vali 2020 & Lopez et al, 2017)

Cross sectional studies  using liver biopsy as a gold standard have demonstrated that all 3 components of the ELF panel increase in patients with chronic liver disease and increasing severity of hepatic fibrosis.

Step 2: When Fib-4 is ≥ 1.3
Liver elastography testing using vibration controlled transient elastography (VCTE)

Liver Stiffness Measurement or LSM output of the Vibration Controlled Transient Elastography (VCTE) using VCTE is a semi-quantitative assessment of the liver stiffness severity.  VCTE is determined by detecting the speed of a radiofrequency wave traveling from the instrument probe into the liver and detected in the right costal margin area.

A VCTE exam is an office based point of care test that requires the patient to be recumbent and fasting for at least 3 hours. A VCTE exam can be performed in < 10  minutes by an experienced operator with immediate test results.

A VCTE provides the LSM measured in kilopascals which is directly proportional to the amount of scar tissue in the liver. The dynamic range of VCTE testing using the VCTE is 3 to 75 kPA while the dynamic range with other devices differs (i.e. Velacur). A reliable study is defined as the 10 measurements having an interquartile range of < 30% that is calculated by the instrument.
Step 2: When Fib-4 is ≥ 1.3
Liver elastography testing using vibration controlled transient elastography (VCTE)
Contraindications to VCTE testing include the known presence of ascites or a tumor in the right lobe of the liver.

Unreliable VCTE may be seen in patients with Obesity Class I and higher (BMI > 30 kg/m2), those with heart failure or fluid overload or are hemodynamically unstable. It underperforms in Hispanic individuals and also has a high variability between reads. (Caussy et al, 2017, Xu et al, 2023, Ajmera et al, 2023, Tincopa et al, 2024 & Pierce et al, 2024)

A VCTE can also provide a semiquantitative assessment of the extent of hepatic steatosis via determination of the Controlled Attenuation Parameter (CAP) score measured in dB/min. CAP score of 288dB/m is the optimal cut-off to identify hepatic steatosis.
The VCTE is approved by the FDA for clinical use of non-invasive evaluation of hepatic fibrosis and steatosis severity in a variety of chronic liver diseases.

Foundational Management of all MASLD Patients

Knowledge of the interplay between MASLD and cardiometabolic disease empowers the primary care provider to optimize both pharmaceutical management that may provide overarching benefits, as well as guide lifestyle change recommendations.
Let’s review some of the opportunities primary care providers have to make positive impacts on their patients with MASLD in addition to other cardiometabolic disease states:
Healthy lifestyle changes are foundational in MASLD

Intense lifestyle intervention, which included 750 Kcal deficit diet, 200 min per week of walking and behavioral health sessions every 8 weeks, demonstrated that a 5-7% weight loss resulted in reduction in inflammation and 7-10% weight loss showed fibrosis regression as well (Vilar-Gomez et al, 2015).
Healthy lifestyle changes are foundational in MASLD
MASLD Therapy: Dietary Recommendations

Physical Exercise: aerobic or anaerobic (resistance) exercise, 3 times a week, 40-min sessions, as soon as 12-weeks later, shows improvement in BMI, ALT and intra-hepatic fat. (Hashida et al, 2017 & Babu et al, 2021)

Dietary Habits: The Mediterranean diet, combined with sustained weight loss and regular physical activity, is the most effective and evidence-based approach to treating MASLD. It targets the root metabolic dysfunction, improves liver outcomes, and reduces cardiovascular risk — making it the therapeutic foundation before pharmacologic options are considered.

Minimize the use of steatogenic medications

A number of prescription medications may lead to inadvertent fat accumulation in the liver.  These medications should be minimized whenever possible in patients with MASLD and clinically significant fibrosis:
Corticosteroids
Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitor (NRTI)
Didanosine
Stavudine
Zidovudine
Fialuridine
Amiodarone
Methotrexate
Tamoxifen
5-Flurouracil
Irinotecan
(Rinella et al, 2023 & Samala et al, 2018)
Healthy lifestyle changes are foundational in MASLD

The role of the gastroenterologist/hepatologist includes more comprehensive liver risk stratification, exclusion of other liver diseases, and a focus on liver-directed therapy. Close communication between gastroenterology/hepatology and primary care or endocrinology facilitates multidisciplinary management of metabolic comorbidities as well as the prioritization of medications or interventions that may also offer liver benefits.

All patients should undergo dietary/nutritional assessment and a plan established for regular follow-up independent of gastroenterology/hepatology visits. The need for more specialized obesity management, including bariatric surgery referral, health psychology, and additional cardiology or lipid metabolic support, should be assessed on an individual basis.
Chronic Disease and Preventive Measures for Primary Care Consideration in MASLD Patients
Awareness of the evidence-based MASLD clinical practice guidelines is the first step in helping to improve clinical outcomes. (Cusi, et. al 2025, Rinella et al, Hepatology 2023)

Knowledge of the interplay between MASLD and cardiometabolic disease empowers the primary care provider both to optimize pharmaceutical management that may provide overarching benefits, as well as guide lifestyle change recommendations.

There are currently 2 FDA-approved medications for MASH patients with F2 to F3 fibrosis (resmetirom, semaglutide).  Side effects of these medications may drive some of these patients to their primary care provider for evaluation.
Some of these medications may lead to inadvertent drug-drug interactions (Madrigal Pharmaceuticals, Inc., 2024).

Type 2 Diabetes & Pre-diabetes in MASLD Patients
: Management of Type 2 Diabetes & Pre-diabetes with Glucose-lowering medications
There are glucose-lowering medications that have been found to have beneficial or potentially beneficial effects for hepatic steatosis, MASH, and/or regression of liver fibrosis. (Cusi, et al., 2025)
In mid-August of 2025, the FDA approved one of the brand names of semaglutide (Wegovy®) for treatment of MASH with moderate-to-advanced liver fibrosis in the adult patient population (FDA, 2025)
An ongoing phase 3 trial discovered that 63% of participants had histologically proven resolution of MASH. The trial is ongoing. (FDA, 2025)

Guidelines recommend that FDA-approved type II diabetes medications that have been shown to be safe and effective for MASH be given preference for the treatment of adults with type II diabetes with MASLD (Cusi, et al., 2025)
Chronic Disease and Preventive Measures for Primary Care Consideration in MASLD Patients
Optimize Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in MASLD patients:
Dyslipidemia in MASLD 1
Statins are a well-established part of the treatment armamentarium for primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention in patients with diabetes
Dyslipidemia is one of the many factors that contributes to the hepatic steatosis and inflammation of  MASLD  (da Silva Pereira, Franco, Santos, & Daliry, 2025)

Statins have been shown to possess antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, which may help benefit inflammation and fibrosis in the liver of patients with MASLD beyond the direct lipid lowering effects. (Gratacos-Gines & Pose, 2023)  (da Silva Pereira, Franco, Santos, & Daliry, 2025)

No FDA-approved indication for statins as a hepatoprotective agent; however, when used as indicated and approved for patients with cardiovascular risk factors, would help in optimizing dyslipidemia, a known cardiometabolic risk factor for MASLD.
Chronic Disease and Preventive Measures for Primary Care Consideration in MASLD Patients
Optimize Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in MASLD patients:
Dyslipidemia in MASLD 2
Statins can be used according to approved indications in patients with liver fibrosis and compensated cirrhosis  (Francis & Forman, 2020)
Caution, consideration for dose reduction, and close monitoring is indicated if statin therapy is utilized by a patient with decompensated cirrhosis (Gratacos-Gines & Pose, 2023).
If a statin is felt to be appropriate for a patient with decompensated cirrhosis, supervision by a hepatologist is advised, as there may be greater risk with less benefit (Francis & Forman, 2020)
Rosuvastatin and pravastatin are hydrophilic statins, thus undergo less hepatic metabolism and are associated with less muscle toxicity risk (Gratacos-Gines & Pose, 2023)
The cardiovascular (and potentially hepatic) benefits of statin therapy outweigh the clinical risks in patients without liver cirrhosis (Francis & Forman, 2020)
Chronic Disease and Preventive Measures for Primary Care Consideration in MASLD Patients
Optimize Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in MASLD patients:
Obesity in MASLD

Weight loss via dietary interventions improves MASLD  disease severity, beginning with  improvement in steatosis and inflammation with 3% - 5% weight loss and fibrosis with 5% - 10% weight loss. (Gomez.  Gastro 2017)
Semaglutide, liraglutide, and tirzepatide are FDA-approved for diabetes mellitus and chronic weight management in those with obesity or who are overweight with 1+ weight-related comorbidity

Optimize Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in MASLD patients:
Alcohol Cessation Counseling
Screening and monitoring for alcohol use is important, as even low alcohol use in those with MASLD can be detrimental  (Marti-Aguado, et al., 2024)

Given the risk alcohol poses to hepatic health in patients with MASLD, screening for and monitoring of alcohol use is important. Examples of simple and quick survey tools for primary care include (National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, 2025):
The Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Consumption (AUDIT-C)
The NIAAA Single Alcohol Screening Question (SASQ)
